Suddenly the anti-EU left wants in all because it fears the British voters

In case of paywall:

Long before the official start of the EU referendum campaign, I paid a visit to the newly opened office of the Vote Leave campaign. The smartly dressed young men and women looked like the sort of volunteers one might expect to see at a Conservative party campaign office. But the huge Vote Leave logo across the wall was in exactly the same shade of red associated with Labour election posters. When I pointed this out, one of the volunteers smiled: “That’s not a coincidence.”

Well, of course it isn’t. And it might help explain why, according to recent research, only about half of traditional Labour voters realise their party’s policy is to back the campaign led by David Cameron to keep the UK in the European Union.

There might be another reason for this confusion: their party leader, Jeremy Corbyn, had been a steadfast opponent of our membership of the EU for more than 40 years. His backing for the official Labour “remain” campaign has all the sincerity of a hostage’s confession — though in his case the duress was simply being told by his senior colleagues that none of them would serve in his shadow cabinet unless he performed a volte-face on the issue.

But, like the resourceful hostage in such situations, Corbyn tries to let the outside world know that he doesn’t mean what he is saying. So when a journalist asks him whether he has changed his long-held opinions — for example, in 2011, that “the Eurocrats are presiding over an economic realignment at the expense of all the progress made by the working class over the past 50 years” — he replies: “We’ve agreed as a party on a strategy and a position . . . I’m leading the party in that and I’m on this [campaign] bus at the moment and a very nice bus it is too.” Short of winking, there was not much more he could have done.

Actually, Corbyn did attempt outright sabotage last week, when in a speech standing under the giant hashtag #LabourInForBritain, he rubbished the claims of David Cameron and George Osborne that our economy would be devastated by Brexit as “hysterical hype” and “prophecies of doom”.

I can understand why Corbyn, under the peculiar pressures that come from trying to lead a parliamentary party with very few Eurosceptics, has decided it’s necessary to humiliate himself. It’s less easy to understand why so many of the leading voices of the left in the media have adopted the same self-emasculating approach.

So, for example, Paul Mason — who spent months furiously broadcasting from Athens about the way the Greeks had been forced by the EU to accept debt repayment terms that they had rejected in a referendum — appeared on BBC’s Question Time a couple of weeks ago to say that while he had wanted the UK to leave “because it’s impossible for the European Union to be a democracy”, he would not now back the Brexit campaign.

And last week, on the same programme, The Guardian’s Owen Jones — who after the crushing of Greek resistance to the financial repression of the eurozone wrote an article headlined: “The left must put Britain’s EU withdrawal on the agenda” — also declared he was backing the campaign for the UK to remain part of what less than a year earlier he had denounced as an undemocratic conspiracy against the working class.

So how do these principled fellows explain their remarkable retreat from the barricades of left-wing resistance to the power-brokers of the eurozone, and their support for a British “remain” vote that would come as an almighty relief to the Eurocrats? The existence of Boris Johnson. Really.

Or, as Mason wrote in The Guardian: “Here’s the practical reason to ignore [the principled left-wing case for Brexit]. In two words: Boris Johnson.” The argument — for what it is worth — is that if the UK votes to leave the EU, Boris Johnson will become prime minister and will take the country in a more right-wing direction than David Cameron.

Even if Boris were to succeed Cameron in such circumstances, it is bizarre that anyone on the radical left should discern such a difference between the two Tories’ political views as to justify a country-defining switch on a matter of fundamental principle. Frankly, even most Tory MPs can’t see much difference between Cameron’s and Johnson’s politics — let alone Labour voters.

In any case, wouldn’t the British electorate, in 2020 at the absolute latest, have the chance to boot out a man Mason describes as one of “a bunch of crazed, right-wing Conservatives”? I mean, why would the British people not want to rid themselves of such an alleged lunatic, especially as he would have become prime minister, like Gordon Brown, without the consent of the wider electorate?

Now we are getting to the heart of the matter: which is that those on the radical left who embrace the Labour leadership of Jeremy Corbyn have a profound fear of the British electorate.

Put simply, they don’t trust the people to make the “right” decision when confronted with the choice between — in this case — Jeremy Corbyn and Boris Johnson. And given Johnson managed twice to persuade predominantly Labour-voting Londoners to elect him as their mayor, one can understand their fear.

What this means in practice — and it applies to almost the entire parliamentary Labour party, including the depleted band of Blairites — is they see Brussels as a way of getting the sort of social legislation they want via EU directives, imposed on the recalcitrant British who have had the lamentable bad taste to reject a left-wing platform at the ballot box.

In fact, the extent to which Brussels has been the author of social policy reform in the UK is widely exaggerated. Laws against discrimination by race or gender were pioneered by elected British governments; the minimum wage did not come from Brussels; and for 35 years before joining the EU, the UK had legislation guaranteeing paid holidays.

Even if that were not the case, Corbyn and his supporters in the media need to read again the speech made by Tony Benn a quarter of a century ago, when arguing in the House of Commons against the Maastricht treaty: “Some people genuinely believe that we shall never get social justice from the British government, but that we shall get it from Jacques Delors. They believe that a good king is better than a bad parliament. I have never taken that view.”

Now that the European Commission is run not by a socialist — which Delors was — but by a right-of-centre former prime minister of Luxembourg , the position advanced by the previously Eurosceptic British left is not just undemocratic and unprincipled: it is actually delusional.

As for the Labour party, it should probably be grateful that its voters are so far unaware just how unreflectively supportive it is of Britain’s membership of the European Union and that it remains, institutionally, of the view expressed by Gordon Brown: that anyone hostile to the right of all the inhabitants of the 28 EU member states to live in the UK must be “bigoted”.

The Tories are now experiencing ferocious internecine disputes over the EU referendum: but it might be Labour that pays the highest price — for being united in a cause to which its own core voters are indifferent or actually hostile.
